title: Architecture Data Analysis + Visualization Primer
text:
Bootstrapped confidence intervals (beginner-friendly)
Resample with replacement to estimate uncertainty without heavy math.

def bootstrap_ci(x, n_boot=2000, ci=0.95, seed=42):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    means = []
    for _ in range(n_boot):
        sample = rng.choice(x, size=len(x), replace=True)
        means.append(np.mean(sample))
    lo = np.percentile(means, (1-ci)/2*100)
    hi = np.percentile(means, (1+(ci))/2*100)
    return float(np.mean(means)), float(lo), float(hi)

for cond in ['A','B']:
    m, lo, hi = bootstrap_ci(pilot.loc[pilot.condition==cond, 'dwell_time_mean_min'].values)
    print(cond, 'mean≈', round(m,2), 'CI', (round(lo,2), round(hi,2)))

title: Week 11: Studio Evidence Package Workshop
text:
A4 Has Four Parts

studio decision brief
evidence board / object card
pathway artifact
method appendix

Each part should reinforce the others. If one part contradicts or ignores another, the package reads as unfinished.

title: Week 11: Studio Evidence Package Workshop
text:
The 60-Second Audience Test
A computational pipeline can produce a result without establishing which design response is justified.
Swap your draft package with a partner. They read for 60 seconds, then answer:

what decision is at stake?
what does the author recommend?
how confident should I be?

If they cannot answer all three, the package is not ready for its audience.

title: Week 11: Studio Evidence Package Workshop
section: Review Question 1: Is the Decision Context Clear?
text:
Review Question 1: Is the Decision Context Clear?
Good enough: a reader who has never seen your project can name the decision in one sentence after reading the brief.
Common failure: the brief opens with method or background instead of the decision. The reader reaches the recommendation without knowing what was being decided.
Fix: write the decision as the first sentence. Everything else follows from it.

title: Week 11: Studio Evidence Package Workshop
section: Review Question 2: Does the Evidence Support the Recommendation?
text:
Review Question 2: Does the Evidence Support the Recommendation?
Good enough: each piece of evidence in the package connects to the recommendation through a stated reason, not just proximity on the page.
Common failure: the evidence is real, but the recommendation could be swapped for the opposite and nothing in the package would contradict it.
Fix: for each figure or data point, write one sentence: “this supports the recommendation because ________.” If nothing fills the blank, the evidence is decoration.

title: Week 11: Studio Evidence Package Workshop
section: Review Question 3: Is the Pathway Visible?
text:
Review Question 3: Is the Pathway Visible?
Good enough: a reader can tell which tool produced the evidence and could, in principle, rerun the workflow.
Common failure: the pathway artifact exists but is disconnected from the brief. The spreadsheet, map, or notebook sits in an appendix that no one reads.
Fix: reference the artifact directly in the brief: “the comparison in Figure 2 was produced by ________.”

title: Week 11: Studio Evidence Package Workshop
section: Review Question 4: Are the Limits Stated Directly?
text:
Review Question 4: Are the Limits Stated Directly?
Good enough: the package names at least one thing the evidence does not establish and one condition under which the recommendation might change.
Common failure: limits appear as a disclaimer paragraph at the end that reads as boilerplate rather than genuine reflection.
Fix: embed limits next to the claims they qualify. “This comparison covers three sites; a fourth with different transit access might change the ranking.”

title: Week 11: Studio Evidence Package Workshop

High Line, New York

title: Week 11: Studio Evidence Package Workshop
text:
Demonstrated vs. Validated
A working pipeline is not a validated claim.
Go through your A4 and mark each claim:

demonstrated: “the workflow runs and produces this output”
validated: “the output has been checked against independent evidence”

Most student work is demonstrated, not validated. That is fine — but say so. Overselling a demonstration as validation is the fastest way to lose a reviewer’s trust.

Option

title: Week 5: BIM, BEM, and Building Performance
text:
What Are BIM and BEM?
BIM

digital model of physical and functional building characteristics
serves design, construction, coordination, and facility management
prioritizes geometry, materials, relationships, and documentation

BEM

computational model of thermal behavior and energy flows
serves analysis, optimization, and compliance
prioritizes zones, schedules, systems, weather, and performance assumptions

Why Not Web Mercator?
Why 2326 (Hong Kong 1980 Grid) and not Web Mercator (3857):

at Hong Kong’s latitude, distances in 3857 are inflated by roughly 8%
a “400 m” buffer in 3857 lands around 370 m on the ground
always buffer in a projected local CRS

This is exactly the kind of silent error the “inspect” step exists to catch.

text:
ARCH7476 is a mixed-cohort course for architecture students who need a clearer way to move from intuition to evidence. Thesis and current-studio decisions are explicitly welcome as the semester project — the course is designed to run alongside them. title: Assignment 1: Evidence Audit + Next Decision Brief
text:
Part 1: Prior Decision Description (about 1 page)
Choose one decision you already made in studio, research, or practice. It should be specific enough that someone could understand what alternatives existed.
Decisions from your current thesis or studio project are explicitly welcome — the course is designed to run alongside them, and the strongest A4 packages usually feed a live project.
Address:

what the design decision was
when it was made
what alternatives were in play
who the decision was for
what constraints mattered most

Examples:

choosing a facade proportion
locating an entrance
deciding between two site strategies
selecting a shading or glazing approach
choosing a circulation layout or public-space arrangement
crumbs: A1: Evidence Audit + Next Decision Brief

title: Assignment 1: Evidence Audit + Next Decision Brief
text:
Part 2: Evidence Audit (about 1-1.5 pages)
Break down what informed that decision at the time.
For each input, explain:

what it was
where it came from
whether it was measured, observed, simulated, cited, assumed, or inferred — or tested by making (a variant, sketch series, or mockup you produced in order to find out)
how strongly it really supported the final move

Your audit should identify:

evidence that was genuinely useful
evidence that was weak but treated as strong
gaps that you ignored or could not address
places where aesthetic judgment or convenience filled the gap
crumbs: A1: Evidence Audit + Next Decision Brief

title: Assignment 1: Evidence Audit + Next Decision Brief
text:
Part 3: Confidence and Limits (about 0.5-1 page)
Reflect on the quality of the earlier decision.
Address:

what you would still defend
what you would now question
what evidence would have changed the decision
whether the decision was reversible, risky, or consequential
crumbs: A1: Evidence Audit + Next Decision Brief

title: Assignment 1: Evidence Audit + Next Decision Brief
text:
Part 4: Next Decision Brief (about 1 page)
Now pivot to an upcoming studio or design question.
Define:

the next decision you expect to make
the main stakeholder or audience
why evidence would help
what kind of evidence would matter most
which of the three course pathways seems most promising right now: spreadsheet, GIS, or Python

You are not locking the pathway yet. You are making an early judgment that A2 will test.

title: Assignment 3: Method Prototype
text:
Due: End of Week 8
Weight: 25% of final grade
Length: 4-6 pages + pilot artifact
Expected effort: roughly 12-20 hours outside class, pathway-dependent
Format: PDF submission plus working files or exported artifact

title: Assignment 3: Method Prototype
text:
Learning Objectives
By completing A3, you will be able to:

Turn a pathway choice into a concrete workflow
Run a pilot using real or realistically structured data
Identify failure points, missing inputs, and weak assumptions
Express uncertainty without collapsing the argument
Document the workflow clearly enough that someone else could follow it

title: Assignment 3: Method Prototype
section: Part 1: Prototype Goal and Scope (about 1 page)
text:
Part 1: Prototype Goal and Scope (about 1 page)
Define:

the specific question the prototype will test
why this is the right slice of the larger project
what counts as success for the pilot
what is intentionally out of scope

Your pilot’s dataset may be your own design alternatives — two or three variants scored, simulated, or walked through under identical conditions. Generated design-variant sweeps (for example, parametric model output) are admissible inputs; the analysis remains what is assessed.

title: Assignment 3: Method Prototype
text:
Part 2: Workflow Description (about 1.5-2 pages)
Describe the workflow step by step.
Include:

input sources and file types
how data is cleaned or structured
core analysis steps
the final output the workflow produces
where judgment enters the process

Where feasible, include at least one real source — DATA.GOV.HK, department datasets, OpenStreetMap, or your own site observations. Pilots that run only on the provided synthetic data should say why.
Examples by pathway:

Spreadsheet

comparison table
filtering and grouping
charting with error ranges or scenario bands
decision matrix



GIS

load layers
confirm CRS and geometry validity
select, join, buffer, or overlay
plot or export a map / spatial summary



Python

open notebook
load and inspect data
transform, summarize, or compare
create plots or exported tables

title: Assignment 3: Method Prototype
text:
Part 3: Pilot Results (about 1-1.5 pages)
Show what the workflow actually produced.
Include:

one or more outputs from the workflow
what those outputs suggest
whether they are already useful for the decision
what remains too weak, noisy, partial, or unresolved

title: Assignment 3: Method Prototype
section: Part 4: Assumptions, Risks, and Uncertainty (about 1 page)
text:
Part 4: Assumptions, Risks, and Uncertainty (about 1 page)
State clearly:

what assumptions the workflow depends on
which inputs are incomplete or low confidence
what errors or ambiguities appeared
what was missing, malformed, or surprising in the data itself, and how you handled it
how those issues affect the strength of the output

title: Assignment 3: Method Prototype
text:
Part 5: Prototype Artifact
Submit one working artifact appropriate to the pathway:

spreadsheet workbook or export
GIS project output or exported map
Jupyter notebook or equivalent export

The artifact does not need to be polished. It needs to be interpretable.

title: Assignment 3: Method Prototype

Workflow Coherence (35%)

Does the prototype form a real end-to-end workflow?
Are inputs, steps, and outputs clearly connected?
Is the pathway being used appropriately?
Are the analysis steps valid for the structure of the data (independence, unit of analysis, sample size) — or are violations explicitly identified?

title: Assignment 3: Method Prototype

Does the output help answer the decision question?
Is the prototype informative even if incomplete?
Are success and failure interpreted thoughtfully?
If the pilot compares the student’s own alternatives, were the comparison conditions held constant?

title: Assignment 3: Method Prototype

Are assumptions and uncertainties named directly?
Does the student avoid overclaiming from a partial prototype?
Are next refinements logically motivated?

Can another student or reviewer understand the workflow?
Is the prototype artifact readable and organized?

title: Week 4 (Alt): GIS in Grasshopper
text:
Step 2a: Import Points
Grasshopper node chain:

File Path → path to points.csv
Read File → raw text
Split Text (separator: \n) → one item per row
List Item (index 0) → discard header row; use Shift List (shift = 1)
For each row: Split Text (separator: ,)
List Item index 1 → x, index 2 → y
Construct Point (x, y, 0)

You now have a point cloud of centroids in Rhino space.

title: Week 4 (Alt): GIS in Grasshopper
text:
Step 2b: Import Polygons
For polygons.csv (columns: id, ring, x, y):

Read File → Split Text by \n → skip header
Parse each row: split by , → extract id, x, y
GHPython component to group vertices by id:

# GHPython: inputs = ids (list), xs (list), ys (list)
# output = polylines (list of point lists)
import rhinoscriptsyntax as rs
import Rhino.Geometry as rg

groups = {}
for i in range(len(ids)):
    fid = ids[i]
    if fid not in groups:
        groups[fid] = []
    groups[fid].append(rg.Point3d(float(xs[i]), float(ys[i]), 0))

polylines = []
for fid in sorted(groups.keys()):
    pts = groups[fid]
    if len(pts) > 2:
        pl = rg.Polyline(pts)
        if not pl.IsClosed:
            pl.Add(pts[0])
        polylines.append(pl.ToPolylineCurve())

a = polylines
Output a → list of closed polyline curves = your site boundaries.

title: Week 4 (Alt): GIS in Grasshopper
text:
Core Operation 1: Buffer
Goal: “What lies within 400 m of each site?”
Grasshopper:

Start from your imported polygon curves
Offset Curve (distance = 400, plane = XY)
Or for points: Circle (radius = 400) at each centroid
Region Union if buffers overlap and you want a merged zone

This replaces sites.buffer(400) from the notebook.

title: Week 4 (Alt): GIS in Grasshopper
text:
Core Operation 2: Clip
Goal: “What part of my data falls inside this boundary?”
Grasshopper:

Import the boundary polygon (e.g., a district outline)
Import the features to clip
Region Intersection (curve A = feature, curve B = boundary)
Or for points: Point In Curve → keep only points that return 1 (inside) or 2 (coincident)

This replaces gpd.clip().

title: Week 4 (Alt): GIS in Grasshopper
text:
Core Operation 3: Spatial Join
Goal: “Which features overlap which zones?”
Use Point In Curve with a GHPython helper:
# GHPython: inputs = points (list), zones (list of curves), zone_names (list)
# output = assignments (list of zone names per point)
import Rhino.Geometry as rg

assignments = []
for pt in points:
    assigned = "none"
    for i, zone in enumerate(zones):
        result = rg.Curve.Contains(zone, pt, rg.Plane.WorldXY, 0.01)
        if result == rg.PointContainment.Inside:
            assigned = zone_names[i]
            break
    assignments.append(assigned)

a = assignments
This replaces gpd.sjoin().

title: Week 4 (Alt): GIS in Grasshopper
text:
Core Operation 4: Dissolve
Goal: “Merge all features that share the same category.”

Group polygons by attribute using GHPython or Create Set
Per group: Region Union → single merged boundary

This replaces gdf.dissolve().

title: Week 4 (Alt): GIS in Grasshopper
text:
Quick Color-by-Attribute Recipe
# GHPython: inputs = values (list of floats), min_val, max_val
# output = colors
import System.Drawing as sd

colors = []
for v in values:
    t = max(0, min(1, (float(v) - min_val) / (max_val - min_val)))
    r = int(255 * (1 - t))
    g = int(255 * t)
    colors.append(sd.Color.FromArgb(r, g, 80))

a = colors
Feed a into Custom Preview → instant choropleth in the viewport.

title: Week 8: Pilot, Compare, and Quantify Uncertainty
section: A Pilot Is Not a Mini Final Project
text:
A Pilot Is Not a Mini Final Project
A pilot is useful if it shows:

the workflow can run
the output is relevant
the assumptions are visible
the weak points are now obvious

A pilot that reveals a problem is more valuable than one that confirms a hope.
crumbs: W8: Pilot, Compare, and Quantify Uncertainty

title: Week 8: Pilot, Compare, and Quantify Uncertainty
text:
Case: The 120-Watt Assumption
Every thermal comfort standard assumes the same thing about a seated office worker:
They produce 120 watts of metabolic heat.
That number enters every PMV calculation, every cooling-load estimate, every energy model. It looks precise. It is not.
crumbs: W8: Pilot, Compare, and Quantify Uncertainty

title: Week 8: Pilot, Compare, and Quantify Uncertainty
section: What Happens When You Replace It
text:
What Happens When You Replace It
A recent study replaced the uniform 120 W assumption with demographic-aware metabolic rates — accounting for age, sex, and body composition.
Results:

simulated HVAC site energy changed by 4–10%
the predicted comfort gap between male and female occupants narrowed by 47%

The assumption looked like a fact. It was a design choice — and it had consequences for who gets comfortable.
crumbs: W8: Pilot, Compare, and Quantify Uncertainty

title: Week 8: Pilot, Compare, and Quantify Uncertainty
section: Why This Matters for Your Pilot
text:
Why This Matters for Your Pilot
Every workflow has a version of the 120-watt assumption:

a default occupant schedule
a standard climate file
a uniform pedestrian speed
a fixed noise threshold

Your pilot should name its assumptions, not hide them inside defaults.
crumbs: W8: Pilot, Compare, and Quantify Uncertainty

title: Week 8: Pilot, Compare, and Quantify Uncertainty
text:
Where Uncertainty Comes From

incomplete data — missing readings, sparse surveys
noisy observations — sensor drift, subjective responses
model assumptions — the 120 W default, fixed schedules
small samples — three sites, not thirty
pseudo-replication — are 120 readings from one room 120 observations, or one?
inconsistent definitions — what counts as “comfortable”?
data treatment choices — how you handle gaps changes the answer
crumbs: W8: Pilot, Compare, and Quantify Uncertainty

title: Week 8: Pilot, Compare, and Quantify Uncertainty
section: Case: Same Data, Different Treatment, Different Conclusion
text:
Case: Same Data, Different Treatment, Different Conclusion
A study of thermal comfort databases encountered missing radiant-temperature readings — a common problem in field research.
Three treatments of the same missing data:



Treatment
Air-to-radiant sensitivity ratio




Rule-based imputation
1.9


Learning through missingness
4.5


Measured-only subset
(different again)



The learning model and validation splits were held fixed. Only the treatment of gaps changed. The interpretation of the same evidence shifted by more than 2×.
crumbs: W8: Pilot, Compare, and Quantify Uncertainty

title: Week 8: Pilot, Compare, and Quantify Uncertainty
text:
The Lesson
It is not enough to say “I cleaned the data.”
You must also ask: would a different reasonable cleaning change my conclusion?
If yes, that is not a flaw in your work. It is an uncertainty you should report.
crumbs: W8: Pilot, Compare, and Quantify Uncertainty

title: Week 8: Pilot, Compare, and Quantify Uncertainty
text:
Probability vs. Point Prediction
Traditional thermal comfort gives you a single number:

“PMV = 0.3, therefore comfortable.”

But research on ordinal learning shows that thermal sensation is better represented as a probability distribution:

“73% probability of neutral or slightly warm, 18% probability of warm, 9% probability of hot.”
crumbs: W8: Pilot, Compare, and Quantify Uncertainty

title: Week 8: Pilot, Compare, and Quantify Uncertainty
text:
Why Probabilities Matter
The point prediction says: this is the answer.
The distribution says: here is how confident you should be.
For your pilot:

a single score hides disagreement
a range or distribution makes the uncertainty visible
your audience can then decide whether the confidence is enough for the decision at hand
crumbs: W8: Pilot, Compare, and Quantify Uncertainty

title: Week 8: Pilot, Compare, and Quantify Uncertainty
text:
Input Quality vs. Model Complexity
Architecture students often invest in more complex models while using default inputs.
A study of climate-adapted weather files found:

the standard weather file (TMY3) had a cool bias that propagated into 16–31% annual heating overestimates in New York
in Los Angeles, the same bias reversed sign — the error went the other direction
historical-file biases — not statistical methods — dominated the tested future-scenario errors

The weather file mattered more than the model.
crumbs: W8: Pilot, Compare, and Quantify Uncertainty

title: Week 8: Pilot, Compare, and Quantify Uncertainty
text:
The Equivalent in Your Work



Over-invested
Under-examined




complex simulation
which climate file?


detailed 3D model
which occupant schedule?


multi-criteria scoring
which weights?


sophisticated GIS layers
which boundary definition?



Before making the model more complex, check whether the inputs deserve the precision.
crumbs: W8: Pilot, Compare, and Quantify Uncertainty

title: Week 8: Pilot, Compare, and Quantify Uncertainty
text:
Case: Equal Setpoints, Unequal Outcomes
A residential cooling study set the same thermostat temperature across all units.
The result: equal cooling setpoints produced unequal modeled thermal outcomes across buildings and age groups.

occupants aged 65+ experienced higher predicted core temperatures in all 24 tested cases
lowering the setpoint helped them but increased cold-discomfort hours for others
predicted sensation and physiological state gave different information

Comparison revealed hidden inequity that the uniform policy concealed.
crumbs: W8: Pilot, Compare, and Quantify Uncertainty

title: Week 8: Pilot, Compare, and Quantify Uncertainty
section: Case: When a Benefit Comes From the Wrong Source
text:
Case: When a Benefit Comes From the Wrong Source
A learned HVAC supervisor was tested against fixed, PMV-based, and adaptive-band policies across 24 scenarios (six cities, two emissions pathways, present and future weather):

it saved 3–7% of site energy in every scenario
but it increased worst-zone warm-temperature exposure in every scenario too

Matched ablations showed that the setpoint bounds — not the learning — drove the savings.
The apparent benefit came from the operating constraints, not the intelligence.
crumbs: W8: Pilot, Compare, and Quantify Uncertainty

title: Week 8: Pilot, Compare, and Quantify Uncertainty
text:
Why Ablation Matters
If you compare option A against option B and A wins, ask:

which part of A produced the benefit?
would a simpler version of A do the same thing?
is the benefit real, or is it an artifact of the comparison setup?

This is the difference between “my method works” and “I know why it works.”
crumbs: W8: Pilot, Compare, and Quantify Uncertainty

title: Week 8: Pilot, Compare, and Quantify Uncertainty
text:
Uncertainty Audit: Your Own Pilot
For your current A3 prototype, answer these five questions:

What is the single most influential assumption?
What happens if that assumption is wrong by 20%?
Are your observations independent, or pseudo-replicated?
Would a different reasonable data treatment change the conclusion?
Does your output report a point value or a range?

Write down the answers. They belong in your A3 submission.
crumbs: W8: Pilot, Compare, and Quantify Uncertainty

title: Week 8: Pilot, Compare, and Quantify Uncertainty
text:
Better Language for Results
Instead of:

“the data proves”
“this shows that”
“clearly demonstrates”

Try:

“the pilot suggests”
“the comparison indicates, subject to [named limit]”
“confidence is limited by [specific source]”
“under these assumptions, the result favors X”
“a different treatment of [gap/input] could change this”

Hedging is not weakness. It is precision.
crumbs: W8: Pilot, Compare, and Quantify Uncertainty

title: Week 8: Pilot, Compare, and Quantify Uncertainty
text:
Comparison Logic
A good comparison requires:

stated criteria — before you compare, not after
controlled differences — change one thing, hold the rest
named assumptions — which defaults are you accepting?
sensitivity check — does the ranking survive a reasonable change in inputs?
provenance — which data came from measurement, which from a model, which from a standard?

If your recommendation changes when one input shifts by 20%, say so.
crumbs: W8: Pilot, Compare, and Quantify Uncertainty

title: Week 8: Pilot, Compare, and Quantify Uncertainty

title: Week 10: Draft Review and Workflow Documentation

title: Week 10: Draft Review and Workflow Documentation
section: Method Transparency: How Much Is Enough?
text:
Method Transparency: How Much Is Enough?
Show just enough that someone can trust the output:

basic workflow — what happened between input and output?
major assumptions — what did you choose that could have gone differently?
main limitation — what should a reader not conclude from this?

The audience does not need your full pipeline. They need enough to judge whether your conclusion is reasonable.
crumbs: W10: Draft Review and Workflow Documentation

title: Week 10: Draft Review and Workflow Documentation
text:
Method Transparency: A Research Example
An HVAC control study tested a learned-probability supervisor against fixed, PMV, and adaptive-band policies across 24 scenarios — six cities, two emissions pathways, present and future weather.
The full method is complex. But the trust-worthy summary is four lines:

data: simulated buildings under 24 climate scenarios
method: compared energy use and thermal exposure across four control strategies
finding: the supervisor saved 3–7% energy but increased worst-zone warm exposure in every scenario
key insight: matched ablations showed setpoint bounds, not the learned model, drove the savings

Your students’ methods are simpler than this. If a 24-scenario study fits in four lines, yours can fit in three.
crumbs: W10: Draft Review and Workflow Documentation

title: Week 10: Draft Review and Workflow Documentation
section: Making Method Visible for a Public Audience
text:
Making Method Visible for a Public Audience
At the 2025 Venice Architecture Biennale, CO₂ measurements from Hong Kong wet markets were overlaid on floor plans through augmented reality.
The audience was not engineers. The method had to be:

visible — viewers could see where readings came from
honest — the sealed retrofit showed ~216 ppm CO₂ above mixed-mode markets
immediate — the trade-off between enclosure, cooling, and fresh air was clear on sight

Your evidence board has the same challenge: make the method visible without making it the story.

title: Python + ML Basics for Architects
text:
A fast, friendly introduction to Python, data handling, and simple machine learning — using fake but architecture-flavored data.
Goals: - Learn Python + pandas basics - Load and explore a dataset about windows/daylight/energy - Split into train/test, fit simple models, and evaluate - Understand cross-validation and overfitting with visuals - Get a small taste of neural nets via an MLP (“deep learning vibe”)

title: Python + ML Basics for Architects
section: Regression: predict cooling energy from design inputs
text:
Regression: predict cooling energy from design inputs
We fit a simple linear model and evaluate on a held-out test set.

features = ['wwr','shading_depth_m','orientation','glazing_u_w_m2k']
target = 'cooling_kwh_m2'
X = df[features]
y = df[target]

cat = ['orientation']
num = ['wwr','shading_depth_m','glazing_u_w_m2k']
pre = ColumnTransformer([
    ("cat", OneHotEncoder(drop='first'), cat),
    ("num", 'passthrough', num)
])

X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.25, random_state=42)
reg = Pipeline([('pre', pre), ('model', LinearRegression())])
reg.fit(X_train, y_train)
pred = reg.predict(X_test)
r2 = r2_score(y_test, pred)
mae = mean_absolute_error(y_test, pred)
r2, mae


plt.scatter(y_test, pred, alpha=0.8)
plt.xlabel('Actual cooling kWh/m²')
plt.ylabel('Predicted')
plt.title(f'Linear Regression: R²={r2:.2f}, MAE={mae:.1f}')
m = np.array([y_test.min(), y_test.max()])
plt.plot(m, m, 'k--', alpha=0.5)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

title: Python + ML Basics for Architects
text:
Classification: comfortable daylight?
Define a simple label: comfortable if glare_probability < 0.35 and daylit_area > 0.5.

df['comfortable'] = ((df['glare_probability'] < 0.35) & (df['daylit_area'] > 0.5)).astype(int)
Xc = df[['wwr','shading_depth_m','orientation']]
yc = df['comfortable']
pre_c = ColumnTransformer([
    ("cat", OneHotEncoder(drop='first'), ['orientation']),
    ("num", 'passthrough', ['wwr','shading_depth_m'])
])
Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(Xc, yc, test_size=0.25, random_state=42, stratify=yc)
clf = Pipeline([('pre', pre_c), ('model', LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000))])
clf.fit(Xtr, ytr)
predc = clf.predict(Xte)
acc = accuracy_score(yte, predc)
cm = confusion_matrix(yte, predc)
acc, cm


confusion_matrix_plot(cm, class_names=("Not Comfortable","Comfortable"), title=f'Logistic Regression (Accuracy={acc:.2f})');

title: Python + ML Basics for Architects
text:
Cross-validation and overfitting
We vary model complexity (polynomial degree) and show CV scores.

deg_scores = []
cv = KFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=42)
for deg in range(1,7):
    poly = PolynomialFeatures(degree=deg, include_bias=False)
    pipe = Pipeline([('pre', pre), ('poly', poly), ('ridge', Ridge(alpha=1.0))])
    scores = cross_val_score(pipe, X, y, cv=cv, scoring='r2')
    deg_scores.append((deg, scores.mean(), scores.std()))

ds = pd.DataFrame(deg_scores, columns=['degree','cv_mean','cv_std'])
plt.errorbar(ds['degree'], ds['cv_mean'], yerr=ds['cv_std'], fmt='o-')
plt.xlabel('Polynomial degree (complexity)')
plt.ylabel('CV R²')
plt.title('Overfitting demo: watch CV score peak then drop')
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
ds


Visualizing CV folds (“crazily simple”)
Each row is a fold; green cells are train, red cells are test.

cv2 = KFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=7)
_ = plot_cv_folds(n_samples=len(X), cv_splits=cv2.split(np.arange(len(X))), title='5-fold CV: train vs test membership')
plt.show()

A tiny taste of “deep learning”: MLP
A small neural network classifier. This is just to build intuition — it’s not magic, and simple models are often enough.

mlp = Pipeline([('pre', pre_c), ('mlp', MLPClassifier(hidden_layer_sizes=(16,8), max_iter=1000, random_state=42))])
mlp.fit(Xtr, ytr)
acc_mlp = accuracy_score(yte, mlp.predict(Xte))
acc, acc_mlp

title: Python + ML Basics for Architects
text:
Key ideas

Always hold out test data or use cross-validation
Start simple; only add complexity if it improves validated performance
Document random seeds and settings for reproducibility
“Deep” models need more data and care; don’t overfit
